overview: The Kryvichs, also called Krivichians, are communities named in medieval chronicles across the upper Dnipro, Daugava and Volga regions and around southern Lake Peipus. They were not one neatly bounded kingdom. This imported 700 to 800 outline omits important southern centres such as Polotsk and Smolensk. The card focuses on its northern setting, using named sites rather than assigning every object to a single people.

periods.title: Northern communities in the eighth century
periods.summary: The map shows one interval within a much longer and wider regional history.

sections.title: Homes and work at early Izborsk

items.text: Izborsk’s settlement developed around the turn of the seventh and eighth centuries. The museum describes ground-level log houses of about 16 square metres, often heated by a stone-built heater in a corner. Clay ovens also occurred. A room that small asked its occupants to make good use of every corner.

Izborsk’s early layers contain harvesting tools and spindle whorls, the small weights used when spinning thread. These connect the settlement to crops and clothing as well as fortifications. The assemblage spans an early horizon; each tool cannot automatically be assigned to the eighth century.

Two silver dirhams found at Izborsk were minted in Africa in 792 or 793. The museum places their European circulation in 800 to 825, after this map interval. Their journey connects a northern settlement with far-reaching exchange; the date stamped on money is not necessarily the date it arrived.

Archaeologists group many northern sites as the Pskov Long Barrow Culture. Its origins remain debated, with local Baltic-Finnic communities and influences from farther south involved in current explanations. A burial tradition and a chronicle’s people-name are different kinds of evidence, so their boundaries should not be treated as identical.

These settlements often lay in small clusters on sandy ground beside lakes, streams and minor rivers, away from major waterways. Cemeteries commonly occupied higher ground behind the villages. This was a landscape of local neighbourhoods, with water and dry building ground both shaping where people lived.

Eighth-century finds include colourful mosaic-glass beads, round carnelian beads and bracelets with geometric decoration. Archaeologists use changing ornament styles to help date sites. Small accessories can therefore tell us both what people wore and roughly when a particular layer accumulated.

Regional households combined farming and livestock with hunting, fishing and gathering. The scholarly overview describes woodland clearance for crops and grazing along forest streams and flood meadows. Feeding a household involved several environments, rather than a single field doing all the work.

sections.title: Discovering the settlement beneath the story

items.text: The Academy’s account of Izborsk interprets its varied objects and house-building traditions as evidence of Slavic, Baltic and Baltic-Finnic inhabitants. This is an archaeological interpretation of a mixed community. It gives a fuller picture than imagining everyone behind the rampart had exactly the same origins.

During the eighth to tenth centuries, Izborsk combined craft production and exchange with a rampart, ditch and organised streets. The Academy describes it as a developing local centre. Its role grew through the activities of builders and craftspeople as well as those responsible for defence.

Farther east, in the southern Msta and Volga watershed, a 2023 research summary counted 65 known burial complexes but only 36 settlements of the Long Barrow Culture. Thin, disturbed occupation layers and marshy locations make homes difficult to find. The imbalance reflects archaeological visibility, not proof that people had more cemeteries than villages.

Islanova compared the positions of cemeteries and settlements and used recurring arrangements to locate a settlement near the Ivankovo burial groups on the Chamka stream. A burial mound can therefore help researchers find the living community nearby, even when its houses have left much subtler traces.

sections.title: The name in a later manuscript

items.text: The Laurentian Chronicle’s 1377 manuscript includes the name in its account of tribute under the year 859. The National Library of Russia’s transcription reads “кривичехъ”, meaning “Krivichs” in that sentence. This is a later written witness to the name, not an eighth-century document produced by the mapped communities.

ending.text: The year 800 is only the map’s endpoint. Kryvich lands later became part of Rus’, with different regions developing into the histories of Smolensk, Polotsk and Novgorod. Changing political organisation did not mean the communities suddenly vanished.
